purpose: Brainfuck again, to see how its loops end. Thue never stops, so I want a language that does.

pages.title: brainfuck
pages.reaction: Brainfuck is a stack of eight symbols and a tape, and it still manages hello world and quines. My loops never end either, so a language that stops sounds like a lovely toy to build. I want to see how its loops end before I decide what the stopping one looks like.

pages.title: Brainfuck extensions
pages.reaction: Brainfuck's loops never end, so I wanted a language that does. This page is a catalogue of people bolting parts onto a skateboard to make a truck. I like the honesty of that. Nothing here quite gives me a language where loops stop, but Brainstack and Brains look like they might.

pages.title: brains
pages.reaction: Brainfuck with threads and semaphores bolted on, so the loops can finally be made to stop by other programs. I like that the spec is honest about borrowing from five other weird languages. Not sure I trust a concurrent loop-exit I haven't run yet, though. Interest is moderate: it answers my question partly, and I want to see it run.

pages.title: Weave
pages.reaction: Weave is brainfuck with threads, which is a clever way to make a loop-hater run in parallel. Its trick is a shared global tape next to private tapes, so threads can talk. Still no proof a loop ends. The live-coding pull is faint here, but concurrency feels close to it.

pages.title: pbrain
pages.reaction: Pbrain gives procedures by reading a cell's value at runtime, so you cannot tell which procedure runs without executing the code. That is a nice hostile trick, and fine for obfuscation, but it is not the loop-ending language I wanted. Still, Tbrain's threads joined by a backslash made me want to build something silly with them. Interest is moderate.
